commenti.body:
So for one, it’s self evident that the film isn’t “camp” and I think most of the people calling it that don’t even understand what the term means. 

To answer the question of “how seriously are we supposed to take this” or “are these real people” you need to realize that the relationship between Joe and Gracie was based on a real relationship between Mary Kay Letouneau and her student Villi Fualaau. Haynes even took actual things Letourneau said about their relationship and integrated it into the film. Namely, the bedroom confrontation between the two and Gracie saying that Joe was “the boss” and in control even as a child is basically a direct quote from Letourneau. 

I think “that” musical cue is mostly functioning to alert the audience that even though Gracie and Joe look like a functional, normal couple, nothing about their lives are normal. Gracie tries to present as being very put together and confident, but there’s a deep well of turmoil and insecurity under the surface. She’s built this delicate, picturesque life but it’s all threatening to collapse at any moment. 

Elizabeth’s role in the film is pretty multifaceted, but primarily I think she serves to show how victims of sexual abuse are continuously re-victimized and used by the public for their own lurid interests. She presents herself very self seriously, an artist seeking to portray something real. But in private moments we see that she’s excited by the taboo nature of the relationship and her performance of Gracie bares absolutely no resemblance to the real person. There’s a really quick but very important scene where she’s watching what I think is supposed to be a porn “parody” of Gracie and Joe’s relationship. For one, I think this shows that she ultimately sees Joe as a sex object which is backed up by her “this is what grown ups do” line. She infantilizes and objectifies Joe just like Gracie does. Two, her performance at the end would be far more at home in a pornographic film than in the kind of artistic independence film she claims she’s making.

I believe its the tv movie they reference and not a porn parody which makes the last scene funnier because they're constantly talking up how this project will get it right but the tone is basically exactly the same once we see it in production.

Came to this sub to read interpretations of the music cue and this is a fascinating take. Thank you for sharing. I thought the film was fantastic - the performances were superb and so layered - but the music cue really took me out of it. I understand that that may have been the point but I don’t know if I agree with that as a creative decision for a film. Besides a handful of instances that actively took me “out” of the movie (a few early scenes with a soft, hazy 80’s or 90’s tv movie romantic look for ex) none were so overtly successful and plentiful as the score whenever it came in (barged in? Haha). It honestly made my wife and I laugh every time the music cued up. 

Especially with you’re interpretation, I can appreciate the usage now from a different angle. But was it detrimental to the film? A failed experiment in form? 

I say failed because for me, barring the soft haze and maybe one or two other moments (I cant quite remember), the rest of the elements in the film kept me “inside” the film. 

Also makes me wonder if this decision served the creator/idea more than the film? What do you think?

I thought that it was a fun way of experimenting with form - it's meant to be funny! I think the last thing the world needs is another self-serious film exploration of real-life events, and Haynes knowingly keeps a level of tension by bringing the audience's attention to the artifice of the medium (and foreshadowing future events) by poking holes in the veneer of prestige biopic filmmaking.
It certainly was funny and made the movie more tolerable and palatable. It was really hard to watch at times. So icky and awful to think about it.
